lead: This unit explains what an operating system is, how it sits between programs and hardware, and how it protects and shares the CPU, memory, storage and devices. After it you can read a boot sequence, trace a system call, compare kernel structures, and explain dual mode, interrupts, services and virtualization in exam terms.
about: The unit builds the vocabulary for the rest of the subject. It begins with what an operating system does and how a computer is organized (1.1), then shows how interrupts and architecture let the CPU switch work (1.2). It traces OS history and types (1.3), explains dual mode and timers (1.4), and lists the services an OS offers (1.5). System calls show the controlled entry into the kernel (1.6). The next chapters compare kernel structures (1.7), follow design, building and booting (1.8), and close with kernel data structures, virtualization and computing environments (1.9). Each chapter uses the previous one, so the unit moves from a single idea—the OS as a protected resource manager—to the concrete mechanisms and structures that implement it.

chapters.idea: The OS is a resource manager and an abstraction layer that hides hardware details from programs.
chapters.depth: Define an OS and its goals: convenience, efficiency, ability to evolve. Cover CPU, memory, storage and I/O as managed resources. Cover process, thread, address space, file and pipe as abstractions. Explain the hardware-software interface and ISA. Some syllabi call this 'role of OS' or 'OS as virtual machine'.

figure.title: OS between apps and hardware
figure.aria: Applications request services through the system call interface; the kernel controls hardware and receives interrupts.

chapters.example: A phone has 8 GB RAM and 8 CPU cores. Four apps each ask for 2.5 GB. Can all four keep their data in RAM at once? Explain the OS role in deciding.
chapters.trap: The OS is not the GUI and not one app; the kernel is only the core part of the OS.
chapters.leave: System call mechanics to Chapter 1.6; virtual memory and paging to Unit 4; process scheduling to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The CPU, memory and I/O devices communicate over buses, and interrupts let devices force the CPU into OS code.
chapters.depth: Cover von Neumann organization, CPU registers, buses and device controllers. Compare polling, interrupt-driven I/O and DMA. Cover interrupt sources, priority, vector table or IDT, ISR, and trap versus interrupt. Mention ARM and Intel briefly. Some syllabi call this 'computer-system architecture' and 'interrupt handling'.

figure.aria: The CPU runs an application until a disk interrupt at 40 ms, handles the request for 15 ms, then resumes the application.

chapters.example: A disk DMA transfer runs for 40 ms while the CPU runs an app. At 40 ms the disk raises an interrupt; the handler takes 5 ms and the ISR takes 10 ms. Draw the CPU and disk timeline to 100 ms.
chapters.trap: An interrupt is not a process; a trap is a software-generated interrupt, often from a system call or an error.
chapters.leave: Device drivers, buffering and disk scheduling to Unit 5; context switch details to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Operating systems evolved from batch systems to multiprogramming, time-sharing, real-time, mobile and distributed systems.
chapters.depth: Cover serial and batch processing, multiprogramming, time-sharing, real-time, distributed, embedded, mobile and open-source systems. Trace generations from vacuum tubes to VLSI and personal computers. Some syllabi call this 'history and evolution of OS' and 'types of OS'.

figure.aria: A timeline showing batch systems, time-sharing, personal computers and mobile operating systems overlapping in different eras.

chapters.example: Draw a timeline with batch 1950-1965, time-sharing 1965-1985, PC 1980-2000 and mobile 2000-2025. Name one main feature of each type.
chapters.trap: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory; multitasking is time-sharing on one user's work; multiprocessing uses more than one CPU.
chapters.leave: Scheduling algorithms to Unit 2; distributed file systems to Unit 6; mobile OS architecture details are only touched here.

chapters.idea: Dual mode and a timer protect the kernel from user programs: the mode bit controls privileges and the timer forces the CPU back to the OS.
chapters.depth: Cover user mode, kernel mode, the mode bit, privileged instructions and the system call trap. Cover timer interrupts and why both mode and timer are needed. Some syllabi call this 'OS operations' or 'dual-mode operation'.

figure.title: Mode switch cycle
figure.aria: A cycle that moves from user mode to a trap, then to kernel mode, and back to user mode after return.

chapters.example: A process starts at t = 0 in user mode. At t = 5 ms it calls read(); the kernel handles it for 2 ms. At t = 10 ms a timer interrupt fires. Trace the mode bit at t = 0, 5, 7 and 10 ms.
chapters.trap: A system call is not a special mode; it is an instruction that traps into kernel mode, which then sets the mode bit to 0.
chapters.leave: Context switching and process states to Unit 2; system call types to Chapter 1.6.

chapters.idea: An OS offers services to users and programs and also keeps the system efficient and protected.
chapters.depth: Cover user services: user interface, program execution, I/O, file-system manipulation, communication and error detection. Cover system services: resource allocation, accounting, protection and security. Cover system programs and CLI or GUI. Some syllabi call this 'OS services' or 'system services'.

figure.aria: A tree that splits OS services into user services such as I/O and files, and system services such as allocation and protection.

chapters.example: A UPI payment of ₹500 opens the app, reads a fingerprint, sends a network request and writes a log. Name the OS services used at each step.
chapters.trap: Services are what the OS provides; system calls are the programming entries used to request them. Protection is internal access control, while security defends against outside attacks.
chapters.leave: System call details to Chapter 1.6; access matrix and security attacks to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A system call is the controlled entry from a user program into the kernel, and calls fall into a few standard types.
chapters.depth: Cover the system call mechanism, system call number, parameter passing in registers or on the stack, and return values. Cover types: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication and protection. Compare API and system call. Some syllabi call this 'system call interface'.

figure.aria: A user program calls read in the C library, the library traps into the kernel, and the kernel returns 6 bytes.

chapters.example: A program calls read(fd, buf, 10). The file has 6 bytes left. Trace the system call path and give the call's type.
chapters.trap: A library function is not always a system call; read returns the number of bytes read, and 0 means end of file.
chapters.leave: Process creation and IPC pipes to Unit 2; file-system implementation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Kernel structure trades performance, size and reliability by choosing how much code runs in kernel mode.
chapters.depth: Cover simple or monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular and hybrid structures. Explain message passing in microkernels and loadable modules. Some syllabi call this 'OS structure' or 'kernel architecture'.

figure.aria: A tree of kernel structures: monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular and hybrid.

chapters.example: Suppose a microkernel has a 20,000-line kernel and 4 user servers; a monolithic kernel has 5,000,000 lines. The file service crashes in both systems. Compare which system is likely to survive and why.
chapters.trap: A microkernel is not automatically faster; message passing adds overhead. Layered design is easier to debug but can be slower.
chapters.leave: Linux and Windows case studies to Unit 6; detailed module loading to Chapter 1.8.

chapters.idea: OS design separates policy from mechanism, and building and booting turn source code into a running system.
chapters.depth: Cover design goals, mechanisms and policies, implementation in C and assembly, APIs, system generation, linkers and loaders, and why applications are OS-specific. Cover boot: firmware, bootloader, kernel load, init or systemd. Some syllabi call this 'building and booting an OS' and 'system boot'.

figure.title: Boot sequence
figure.aria: A boot flowchart from power on through firmware, bootloader, kernel, init and login, with times adding to 10 seconds.

chapters.example: A PC takes 2 s in firmware, 3 s in the bootloader, 4 s loading the kernel and 1 s in init. What is the total time to the login prompt? Draw the boot sequence.
chapters.trap: The bootloader loads the kernel; it is not the whole OS. Firmware is not the OS kernel.
chapters.leave: Process creation to Unit 2; file-system mounting to Unit 5; OS debugging is only introduced here.

chapters.idea: Kernels use standard data structures, and virtualization plus varied computing environments change what an OS must manage.
chapters.depth: Cover arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables and bitmaps as kernel data structures. Cover virtualization with type 1 and type 2 hypervisors and containers. Cover traditional, mobile, client-server, peer-to-peer, cloud, real-time and distributed environments, plus open-source OS. Some syllabi call this 'virtualization' and 'computing environments'.

figure.aria: A tree of computing environments: traditional, mobile, client-server, cloud, real-time and distributed.

chapters.example: A cloud host has 8 cores and 32 GB RAM. It runs 8 VMs, each with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM. Is the host oversubscribed in CPU or memory? Explain using virtualization.
chapters.trap: Virtualization is not emulation; a container shares the host kernel, while a VM runs its own guest kernel. Type 1 runs on hardware and type 2 runs on a host OS.
chapters.leave: Distributed synchronization and distributed file systems to Unit 6; scheduling to Unit 2; memory management to Unit 4.

links: The OS role needs hardware and interrupts to control devices
Interrupt-driven machines made multiprogramming and time-sharing possible
Time-sharing needs dual mode and a timer to protect the kernel
Protected kernel mode makes OS services safe to request
Services are requested through system calls
System calls enter a kernel whose structure decides the path
Kernel structure shapes design, building and booting
A booted kernel runs on data structures and may host virtual machines
